response.text:
BERT4Rec adds learned absolute positional embeddings to item embeddings and predicts from an appended [MASK]. Consequently, deletion followed by compaction changes both content and surviving items’ positions. For fixed-width, left-padded inputs with the inference mask anchored at the last slot, deleting the oldest k items preserves survivor positions; deleting the newest k shifts older survivors right. Equal deletion counts control retained length, but do not control position. This follows from the architecture described in [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.06690).

A documented control is fixed-length, in-place replacement: [Xu et al.](https://csr21.github.io/xu-csr2021.pdf) explicitly preserve history length to avoid length effects, replacing items with alternative catalog items. For this setting, recommended complementary protocols are: replace equal-sized recent/older blocks with the reserved [MASK], retaining original position IDs, attention visibility and final inference-mask position; or perform position-preserving deletion by blocking selected slots as attention keys/values without compacting survivors. Compare the latter against compacted deletion of exactly the same items to measure sensitivity to reindexing. These are proposed adaptations, not established BERT4Rec causal-identification protocols.

Limitations: [MASK] preserves slots but adds learned mask representations; attention deletion changes visible context size and softmax normalization; catalog replacement introduces new content. None provides a neutral absence intervention, and effects can interact nonlinearly. For reproducibility, freeze one checkpoint/category, disable dropout, predefine k and eligible users, fix replacement seeds, and keep candidate sets and original-history exclusion rules unchanged. Report paired HR@10 changes plus target-score/rank changes, uncertainty and category macro-averages. Read the final appended mask, never count(nonpadding)−1. Agreement across interventions supports model content dependence; it does not establish causal effects on real user preferences.
